Kanerva's SDM read weights each stored pointer by the number of neurons in the intersection of two Hamming balls of radius d. | [LIT-368](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-368.md) v2 | A decision-making theory of visual detection | Tanner & Swets (1954), DOI-10.1037/h0058700. Tanner and Swets model visual detection as testing a statistical hypothesis. The observer compares one sample of neural activity with a cutoff, and signal+noise and noise are Gaussian with equal variance, separated by d′ (the mean difference in noise-SD units, defined as the square root of Peterson and Birdsall's d). The cutoff moves along a curve of P_SN(A) against P_N(A) (the curve now called the ROC; for d′ = 1 it passes through (.16, .50), (.50, .84) and (.84, .98)). The optimal operating point is where the slope equals β = [(1−P(SN))/P(SN)]·[(V_N·CA+K_N·A)/(V_SN·A+K_SN·CA)]. The 4AFC prediction is P(C)=∫F(x)³g(x)dx. With three paid observers, d′ estimated from yes-no data predicted 4AFC accuracy. The "false alarms are guesses" (high-threshold) hypothesis is rejected: false-alarm rate correlated with chance-corrected thresholds (ρ = .30, .71, .67; combined p ≪ .001), and all 12 fitted yes-no scatter lines miss the point (1, 1). | Active — read in full 2026-09-30 ([NOTE-316](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-316.md)); worth reading as the founding psychophysics paper of signal detection theory: it is short, it is the first place d′ is named, and it is the first to put the observer on the ROC and to set the likelihood-ratio criterion β from priors and payoffs. For the ideal-observer mathematics it defers entirely to Peterson and Birdsall (1953), and its experiment is small (three observers) with some statistics asserted rather than shown. |
| [LIT-373](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-373.md) v4 | The two dragons of cognition: recursive condensation for predictive processing | Li (2026), DOI-10.3389/fncom.2026.1778902. A "Hypothesis and Theory" essay proposing that the neocortex is a "biological Savitch machine". Alternating expansion ("odd parity") and contraction ("even parity") phases manufacture the disjoint closed sets of Urysohn's Lemma, and storing ("memoizing") the condensed tokens converts exponential search into polynomial "navigation". Its one non-standard formal result, Theorem 2, R(N) ∝ b^{αN} (§5.2.2, p. 11), is stated without proof. There is no data, simulation or model. The two mathematical pillars are misdescribed: Savitch's theorem saves space at the cost of time and does not memoize, and Urysohn's Lemma gives a continuous separator, not a linear one, and is not an "if and only if". | Rejected — re-read jointly with [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and arXiv 2602.07974 on 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-321.md)); Read jointly with [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and the companion StrLT preprint (arXiv 2602.07974), the essay is the cognitive motivation of a coherent programme: structure is discovered by costly search, condensed into frozen tokens, and reused cheaply. It is not just a misuse of two theorems. Read charitably, its mathematical slips are repairable and are not the reason to set it aside: the Urysohn "iff" and linear readout, Savitch as memoisation, the Definition 2 clash. The reason is what is left after repair: an amortised-inference and complementary-learning-systems picture already in the literature it cites; a neural mapping whose predictions do not discriminate it from standard consolidation accounts; one original quantitative claim, Theorem 2, that is not argued. A reader who wants the programme should read [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and the companion, where it is made precise. |

| [LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md) | The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex | Damasio (1996), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1996.0125. States the somatic marker hypothesis: ventromedial prefrontal cortex holds learned links between classes of situation and the body states (emotions) that went with them; when a situation recurs, those states are re-enacted, through the body or through an "as if" loop in somatosensory cortex, and mark imagined option-outcome pairs as good or bad, overtly as a feeling or covertly as a bias, so that reasoning works over a pruned space. Evidence summarised: ventromedial patients with intact intellect decide badly in life, lack skin-conductance responses to emotive pictures, and in the gambling task keep choosing the losing decks and show no anticipatory responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the somatic marker hypothesis by its author, with the evidence it then rested on. It is a hypothesis paper: the mechanism (ventromedial prefrontal linkages that re-enact body states, by a "body loop" or an "as if body loop", which then mark options good or bad) is stated, not shown, and the evidence it reports is lesion and skin-conductance work summarised from other papers, without numbers. Its strongest piece, that ventromedial patients lack anticipatory skin-conductance responses in the gambling task while responding normally to the losses themselves, is reported here in one paragraph; the 1997 Science report filed alongside it is the place to see that result. Whether the account is true is not this note's question. |

IIT 3.0 states five axioms of experience (existence, composition, information, integration, exclusion), turns each into a postulate about mechanisms in a state, and identifies an experience with the maximally irreducible conceptual structure of a "complex". Exclusion makes a complex a local maximum of integrated conceptual information Φ over all overlapping sets of elements, so complexes cannot overlap and no subset or superset of a complex is conscious. Worked logic-gate examples show minor complexes beside a major one, an inactive network that is conscious, a minimally conscious photodiode, and a feed-forward "zombie" functionally equivalent to a conscious system. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-365.md)), equations excepted; worth reading as the formal statement of the exclusion postulate that Schwitzgebel's 2014 manuscript ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)) attacks: "of all overlapping sets of elements, only one set can be conscious", a complex being a local maximum of Φ against every overlapping set. It is IIT's anti-nesting principle, stated as a postulate and motivated only by the phenomenological exclusion axiom; the paper's Occam's-razor argument is given for exclusion within a mechanism, not between systems. It also says plainly that function does not fix consciousness, which is IIT's answer to whether agency built from parts brings experience with it. |
| [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md) | Self models | Metzinger (2007, rev. 2013), Scholarpedia 2(10):4174. There is no substantial self, only a phenomenal self-model (PSM): the conscious part of an organism's self-model, an instrument of global control. A phenomenal self arises "if and only if a system operates under a transparent PSM", one it cannot introspectively recognise as a model; a first-person perspective is a transparent model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Self-models can be unconscious and artificial, as in Bongard, Zykov and Lipson's limping starfish robot; embodiment comes in three orders, the third conscious. Full-body illusions are offered as the experimental handle. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-372](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-372.md)); worth reading as Metzinger's own short, open statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT) behind Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)): there is no self, only a phenomenal self-model, and a system experiences itself as a self when that model is transparent, that is, when it cannot introspectively recognise it as a model. It is an encyclopedia article, not an argument: the central claim is stated as a definition with a prediction attached, its empirical examples are cited, and the online text is a revision later than the 2007 acceptance, with editing slips. |
| [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | Gallagher (2000), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 4(1):14–21. Divides philosophical accounts of the self into the "minimal self", accessible to present self-consciousness without temporal extension, and the "narrative self", extended in time through memory and story. The minimal self splits into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which come apart in involuntary movement and, after Frith, in schizophrenic thought insertion when a forward comparator fails. Neonatal imitation suggests an embodied minimal self; Strawson's and Tani's are momentary. Against Dennett's narrative centre, the self is "the sum total of its narratives". Read in the author's preprint. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md)), in the author's preprint, not the typeset article; worth reading as the paper that set the minimal self against the narrative self for cognitive science, and for the split of the minimal self into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which it ties to Frith's comparator model of schizophrenic thought insertion. It is a short review: the empirical support is cited, not shown, and its own proposal, the self as "the sum total of its narratives", is offered in two paragraphs. |
| [LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md) | Being No One: The Self-Model Theory of Subjectivity | Metzinger (2003), MIT Press. Per its publisher, "no such things as selves exist in the world: nobody ever had or was a self. All that exists are phenomenal selves", and the phenomenal self is "the content of a 'transparent self-model'". A representationalist and functional analysis of the conscious first-person perspective, with conceptual "tools", constraints on consciousness and neurophenomenological case studies (agnosia, neglect, blindsight, hallucination), asking whether being someone can be analysed at subpersonal levels. Unread: registered from the description and the contents; the theory is read in [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text of the book could be reached. The MIT Press Direct edition is not open access and no author copy is posted. Its theory is read in Metzinger's own short statement, "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md), read in full), and more fully in his "Précis: Being No One" (PSYCHE 11(5), 2005; LIT-568, read in full 2026-10-03), the read substitute for the book, which sets out six of its ten constraints and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), Frontiers in Psychology 5:518. Impulsive action is non-deliberate but purposive. Automatic appraisal of an event's pertinence to the agent's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to establish, modify or end a relation to the object, with "control precedence" (urgency, persistence, attentional capture). Modes of action readiness are what distinguish one emotion from another. Events usually draw several appraisals and so several states of readiness, and their interaction regulates action: much emotion regulation is itself emotional, not reason overriding passion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-433.md)); filed in place of Frijda's The Emotions ([LIT-546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-546.md)), which could not be read, as the shortest lawfully readable statement of his action-readiness theory in his own words. Appraisal of an event's pertinence to one's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change one's relation to the object, which has "control precedence". Modes of action readiness correspond to emotions (hostility to anger, avoidance to fear). Much emotion regulation is itself one state of action readiness checking another, so "there is no clear distinction between processes of emotion and processes of emotion regulation". It is a theoretical paper with no data, written for impulsive action, so it states the theory's core and not its full range. |
| [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md) | The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization | Barrett (2017), SCAN 12(1):1–23. The brain runs an internal model of the body in the world for allostasis. Its predictions are "concepts" issued from agranular limbic cortex and refined by prediction error. Interoceptive predictions are felt as affect (valence, arousal). An emotion is an instance of categorizing sensation with an emotion concept, built the same way as any perception. Since instances of an emotion are "created by multiple spatiotemporal patterns" (degeneracy), the categories have no neural essences, and the classical view, basic-emotion and causal appraisal theories included, is rejected. Emotions are "constructions of the world, not reactions to it." | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-434](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-434.md)); worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the theory of constructed emotion and of its link to predictive processing. The brain's core task is allostasis, run through an internal model whose predictions are "concepts". An instance of emotion is what happens when the brain categorizes predicted interoceptive and exteroceptive sensation with an emotion concept. On this account emotion categories have no neural "essences", and causal appraisal theories are "highly doubtful". The paper is a theoretical synthesis: its own data are a few figures, and the rest is cited evidence and explicitly labelled hypotheses. |
| [LIT-563](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-563.md) | HDDM: Hierarchical Bayesian Estimation of the Drift-Diffusion Model in Python | Wiecki, Sofer & Frank (2013), Frontiers in Neuroinformatics 7:14. HDDM is an open-source Python package that estimates the drift diffusion model (and the linear ballistic accumulator) by hierarchical Bayesian MCMC: subject parameters drawn from group distributions with informative priors, full posteriors, outlier handling, and regression of parameters on trial-by-trial covariates. A tutorial reproduces a theta-power effect on decision threshold that reverses under subthalamic deep brain stimulation. In simulations hierarchical Bayes recovers parameters and detects effects better than χ²-quantile and maximum-likelihood fitting, most with few trials. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-466.md)); worth reading as the methods paper for HDDM, the Python package that fits the drift diffusion model by hierarchical Bayesian estimation (PyMC, MCMC), with subject parameters drawn from group distributions and trial-by-trial regressions of parameters on covariates such as EEG power. Its simulations show hierarchical Bayes recovering parameters with less error than per-subject χ²-quantile, maximum-likelihood or non-hierarchical Bayesian fits, most of all with few trials, and detecting drift-rate differences and covariate effects more often. The comparisons are the authors' own, on data simulated from the model being fitted, and its hypothesis tests on the group posterior differ from the t-tests used for the other methods. |
| [LIT-565](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-565.md) | The Time Course of Perceptual Choice: The Leaky, Competing Accumulator Model | Usher & McClelland (2001), Psychological Review 108(3):550–592. Perceptual choice as gradual, stochastic accumulation in one unit per alternative, with leakage and lateral inhibition between units and a threshold at zero. For two choices the linearised difference is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with net leak K = k − β; K = 0 recovers the classical diffusion model, and K ≠ 0 bounds asymptotic accuracy. The model fits time–accuracy curves slightly better than diffusion with drift variance, fits Vickers's latency–discriminability data, predicts individual primacy or recency biases confirmed in a new experiment, and yields Hick's law under a constant-accuracy criterion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-449](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-449.md)); worth reading as the source of the leaky, competing accumulator (LCA): one leaky accumulator per alternative, lateral inhibition between them, a threshold-linear floor at zero, and an absolute response criterion. In the linear two-choice case the difference between accumulators is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with net leak K = k − β, so the classical diffusion model is the special case K = 0 and accuracy given unlimited time is bounded whenever K ≠ 0. Its evidence for leakage over drift variance is a modest likelihood advantage on 3 participants (combined ratio about 62 to 1, 7 of 9 curves), and the authors concede that a diffusion model with drift variance, starting-point variance and decision boundaries is hard to tell apart from it. |
| [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger (2005), PSYCHE 11(5), the author's précis of Being No One. Minimal consciousness is a global world-model in a window of presence that cannot be recognised as a model (globality, presentationality, transparency). A phenomenal self is a transparent self-model: "no such things as selves exist in the world". Transparency comes in degrees, and the self-model's opaque partition is what lets humans doubt their own self-representation. The unity of consciousness is a single global functional cluster. A first-person perspective is a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation, and iterating it yields introspective and social intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md)), as the read substitute for Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)), which it summarises in Metzinger's own words. Worth reading as the most complete short statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT): more of the machinery than "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)), in particular the six constraints, the degrees of transparency, and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Phenomenal selfhood is a transparent self-model, "a function realized by a lack of information"; "no such things as selves exist in the world". The unity of a conscious world is a global functional cluster bound by "highest-order binding". It states the theory and its predictions; the evidence is cited, not shown, and the neural sections say how little is known. |
| [LIT-569](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-569.md) | The Physics of Optimal Decision Making: A Formal Analysis of Models of Performance in Two-Alternative Forced-Choice Tasks | Bogacz, Brown, Moehlis, Holmes & Cohen (2006), Psychological Review 113(4):700–765. The pure drift diffusion model implements the SPRT and Neyman–Pearson test, so it is the optimal two-choice decision process. The O-U, mutual inhibition (Usher–McClelland), feedforward inhibition and pooled inhibition (Wang) models reduce to it for balanced parameters; the race model does not. For reward rate, Bayes risk and two accuracy-weighted criteria there is a unique optimal threshold, giving parameter-free optimal performance curves. With biased priors the optimal starting point is proportional to the log prior odds. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-461](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-461.md)), main text and Appendix B in full, Appendix A (the derivations) by section only; worth reading as the paper that puts the two-choice decision models in one frame and ties them to the sequential probability ratio test. The pure drift diffusion model is the continuum limit of the SPRT, so it is the fastest for a given accuracy and the most accurate for a given time. Of six models, all but the race model reduce to it in some parameter range: the Usher–McClelland mutual inhibition model when leak equals inhibition and both are large, the feedforward inhibition model when its inhibitory and excitatory weights are equal. Each reward criterion has a unique optimal threshold, which gives testable optimal performance curves. The optimality results hold for the pure model with stationary evidence and two alternatives. |
| [LIT-576](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-576.md) | The Diffusion Decision Model: Theory and Data for Two-Choice Decision Tasks | Ratcliff & McKoon (2008), Neural Computation 20(4):873–922. A review of the diffusion decision model for fast two-choice tasks, with three new motion-discrimination experiments. Noisy evidence accumulates from a starting point z to one of two boundaries (0, a) at drift v, plus non-decision time and across-trial variability in v, z and Ter. The model fits accuracy and full correct and error RT distributions, and maps difficulty to drift, speed–accuracy instructions to boundary separation and stimulus proportion mainly to starting point. Applications cover aging, aphasia and links to neural firing. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-445](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-445.md)), from the author manuscript in PubMed Central; worth reading as the canonical statement of the diffusion decision model and of what it is for. Two-choice RT and accuracy are decomposed into drift rate (quality of evidence), boundary separation (caution), starting point (bias) and non-decision time, plus across-trial variability in drift, starting point and non-decision time. Three new motion-discrimination experiments show each manipulation landing on its own parameter: difficulty on drift, speed–accuracy instructions on boundaries, stimulus proportion mainly on starting point. Its closing claim, that diffusion models have come "as near to provid[ing] a solution to simple decision making as is possible in behavioral science", is the authors' assessment, not a result. |
| [LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md) | Dynamic Patterns: The Self-Organization of Brain and Behavior | Kelso (1995), Dynamic Patterns: The Self-Organization of Brain and Behavior, MIT Press, xvii + 334 pp. The book-length statement of coordination dynamics. Unread: registered from catalogue records. What the record knows of its content comes from the works that cite it: the coordination potential of the HKB model (reproduced in Kelso 2021, Box 1), absolute versus relative coordination (De Jaegher & Di Paolo 2007, citing p. 98), a chapter on how HKB arose (ch. 3) and one on brain rhythms (ch. 8), per Kelso 2021. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, not read. No lawful full text was found: the book has no DOI, is not listed as open access, and MIT Press's page refused an automated request. Under the owner's rule for books it is supplanted by a shorter work by the same author, Kelso's 2021 retrospective on the HKB model ([LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md)), which was read. It is filed because it is the citation others reach for when they mean coordination dynamics, relative coordination or metastability; De Jaegher & Di Paolo ([LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md)) and Raja et al. ([LIT-598](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-598.md)) both cite it. |
| [LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md) | Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems for behavioral control | Daw, Niv & Dayan (2005), Nature Neuroscience 8(12):1704-1711. Habitual and goal-directed control are model-free ("caching") and model-based ("tree-search") reinforcement learners in dorsolateral striatum and prefrontal cortex. Behaviour follows whichever controller's value estimate is less uncertain under approximate Bayesian versions of each. Simulations reproduce the devaluation data: over-training yields devaluation-insensitive habit, except for actions near reward or in tasks with more actions and outcomes. Both controllers serve the same ends; neither is the "irrational" one. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-459](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-459.md)), supplementary methods not read. Worth reading as the founding statement of model-based versus model-free control as two brain systems, and of arbitration between them by relative uncertainty. Goal-directed (devaluation-sensitive) behaviour is a prefrontal "tree-search" controller, statistically efficient but noisy to compute. Habit is a dorsolateral-striatal "caching" controller, cheap but data-hungry and blind to revaluation. Each controls behaviour when its value estimate is the more certain, which reproduces why over-training produces habits unless the task is complex or the action near the reward. Both controllers pursue "identical rational ends": a rejection of the impulsive-limbic-versus-rational-prefrontal picture. |
| [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md) | Hierarchically organized behavior and its neural foundations: A reinforcement learning perspective | Botvinick, Niv & Barto (2009), Cognition 113(3):262-280. Hierarchical RL groups actions into reusable "options" with their own policies, subgoals and pseudo-reward. That eases the scaling problem by cutting the number of decisions to explore and learn. The paper builds an actor-critic version and maps option identifiers to DLPFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and option-length prediction errors to OFC. Unsuitable options produce negative transfer, so how useful options are discovered is the central open problem. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript; the online appendix with the equations was not read. Worth reading as the bridge between hierarchical reinforcement learning (temporally abstract "options") and the psychology and neuroscience of hierarchically organized behaviour. Options ease the scaling problem of RL by shrinking search and learning to a few decision points. An actor-critic version maps option identifiers to dorsolateral PFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and extended prediction errors to orbitofrontal cortex. The problem it puts first is option discovery: the wrong options cause negative transfer, as in human problem solving. |
| [LIT-584](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-584.md) | Model-based and model-free Pavlovian reward learning: Revaluation, revision, and revelation | Dayan & Berridge (2014), Cognitive, Affective, & Behavioral Neuroscience 14(2):473-492. Pavlovian prediction is not only model-free. A cue that had predicted disgusting salt became instantly "wanted" when a never-experienced salt appetite was induced, before the salt was retasted, which needs a prediction of the outcome's identity revalued against the current bodily state. Over-training may "defocus" outcome representations rather than hand control to a model-free system. Dopamine may carry model-based evaluations. No algorithm for the revaluation is given. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-463](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-463.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript. Worth reading as the argument that Pavlovian prediction, usually modelled as purely model-free, is also model-based. In the "Dead Sea salt" experiment a lever that had predicted a disgusting salt solution became, on first presentation after a novel sodium appetite was induced and before any salt was retasted, nearly as attractive as a sucrose lever, with mesolimbic activation. A cached value cannot do that. The CS must predict the outcome's identity, and its value must be recomputed against the current bodily state. The paper adds "defocusing" of outcome representations as a model-based route to apparent habit, and argues that dopamine can carry model-based evaluations. |
| [LIT-585](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-585.md) | The Expected Value of Control: An Integrative Theory of Anterior Cingulate Cortex Function | Shenhav, Botvinick & Cohen (2013), Neuron 79(2):217-240. Control is allocated by a cost-benefit decision. The expected value of control (EVC) of a candidate control signal is its probability-weighted payoff, with future value discounted, minus an intrinsic cost rising with its intensity. dACC monitors state and outcome information and specifies the identity and intensity of the EVC-maximizing signal. Lateral PFC and subcortical structures implement it. The account integrates conflict monitoring, effort costs and the override of defaults (exploration, foraging, patience). | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-446](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-446.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript. Worth reading as the standard statement that cognitive control is allocated by a cost-benefit decision. The "expected value of control" (EVC) of a control signal, which has an identity (which task) and an intensity (how much), is its expected payoff minus an intrinsic cost that rises with intensity. Dorsal anterior cingulate cortex is proposed to monitor and to specify the EVC-maximizing signal, which lateral PFC and subcortical structures then implement. It is a review and synthesis: the model is stated, not fitted, and the authors say the ingredients are not new. |
| [LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso (2021), Biological Cybernetics 115(4):305–322, a 60th-anniversary retrospective. HKB models bimanual coordination by the relative phase φ, with dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ and potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ: both in-phase and anti-phase are stable for b/a > 1/4, and anti-phase loses stability below it, as observed when movement frequency rises. Noise, symmetry breaking (Δω) and metastability extend it; with Kuramoto's model it becomes a generalized HKB for many agents. The same dynamics is reported within a body, between people and with machines, and in brain activity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md)), from the free-to-read publisher PDF. Filed in place of Kelso's book Dynamic Patterns ([LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md)) and as the read account of the paywalled Haken–Kelso–Bunz paper ([LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md)), both Deferred. Worth reading as Kelso's own short statement of coordination dynamics: the HKB order-parameter equation for relative phase, its stochastic and symmetry-breaking extensions, metastability as relative coordination, the generalized HKB–Kuramoto model, and the claim that one coordination dynamics holds within and between people. It is a retrospective by an author of the model, not a review, and it says so. |
| [LIT-605](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-605.md) | An Accumulator Model for Spontaneous Neural Activity Prior to Self-Initiated Movement | Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene (2012), PNAS 109(42). In Libet's spontaneous movement task, a leaky stochastic accumulator, δx = (I − kx)Δt + cξ√Δt, with weak constant urgency I and a threshold, fitted only to waiting times, reproduces the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96): time-locking to threshold crossings averages up the autocorrelated noise that produced them. Fast responses to random interruptions were preceded by a slow negativity, as predicted. The "neural decision to move now" is the late threshold crossing, about 150 ms before movement, so Libet's inference of an unconscious decision a half-second earlier is unfounded. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-462](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-462.md)); worth reading as the model that reinterprets the readiness potential. A leaky stochastic accumulator with a weak constant input ("urgency"), fitted with three parameters to 14 participants' waiting times in Libet's task, reproduces the shape of the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96) because averaging epochs time-locked to threshold crossings recovers the noise that happened to carry the accumulator there. Its prediction, that fast responses to unpredictable clicks are preceded by a slow negativity, was confirmed (13 participants). On this account the "neural decision to move now" is the threshold crossing about 150 ms before movement, not the onset of the readiness potential, and Libet's inference that the brain decides before awareness is "unfounded". The authors say plainly that this shows the readiness potential could reflect spontaneous fluctuation, not that it does. |
| [LIT-614](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-614.md) | Bayesian model reduction | Friston, Parr & Zeidman (2018; v2 2019), arXiv:1805.07092. A review of Bayesian model reduction: given a fitted full model's prior P, approximate posterior Q and free energy F, the free energy of a model with any other prior P̃ is ln E_Q[P̃/P] + F, and its posterior follows by reweighting Q (Eqs. 9–10). Closed forms are given for Gaussian, Dirichlet, beta, gamma, categorical and multinomial priors. Three worked simulations (sparse regression, cluster pruning in a Gaussian mixture, network discovery in a linear dynamical system) and a review of uses: structure learning, hierarchical (PEB) inversion as a cascade of reductions, and "sleep-like" pruning in active-inference agents. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-477](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-477.md)); worth reading as the reference statement of Bayesian model reduction (BMR): the reduced free energy F[P̃:P] ≈ ln E_Q[P̃/P] + F[P] (Eq. 9), which the authors call a generalisation of the Savage–Dickey ratio "to any new prior", with closed forms for Gaussian, Dirichlet, beta, gamma, categorical and multinomial priors (Eqs. 11–12, Table 1). The Dirichlet form is what lets active-inference agents prune their own likelihood mappings. Its examples are simulations, and its review of applications is of the authors' own lab. |
| [LIT-615](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-615.md) | An Active Inference Approach to Modeling Structure Learning: Concept Learning as an Example Case | Smith, Schwartenbeck, Parr & Friston (2020), Front. Comput. Neurosci. 14:41. A partially observed Markov decision process with eight animal "slots", some starting with flat likelihoods, learns new concepts without feedback: a slot is engaged only when its flat mapping explains a feature combination better than any learned concept. Bayesian model reduction on the learned prior over states then resets slots the data did not need. In 100 runs per condition the true number of concepts won in 45–80% of runs for 4–7 concepts and rarely for 2–3, and in every run when the likelihood was given. The agent also generalises to an unseen animal in one shot, and the paper simulates neural and dopaminergic responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-485](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-485.md)); worth reading as the record's worked example of structure learning in an active-inference agent: "model expansion" by spare hidden-state slots whose flat likelihoods win inference only for a truly novel stimulus, and "model reduction" by applying Bayesian model reduction to the agent's learned prior over states, so that unused slots are reset. It is a proof of concept with eight animals and six features. Reduction recovered the true number of concepts in 45–80% of 100 runs for 4–7 concepts, failed for 2–3, and succeeded every time only when the likelihood mapping was given rather than learned. |
| [LIT-620](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-620.md) | Post hoc Bayesian model selection | Friston & Penny (2011), NeuroImage 56(4):2089–2099. If every model of interest is a full model with a different prior and the same likelihood, the evidence of any reduced model is p(y\|m_F) times the full posterior expectation of p(θ\|m_i)/p(θ\|m_F) (Eq. 3). So the reduced models never have to be fitted. A point-mass reduced prior gives the Savage–Dickey ratio (Eq. 6). Under Gaussian priors and posteriors the reduced free energy and posterior are closed-form in the full model's means and precisions (Eq. 9). In simulations an exhaustive search over 4,096 linear models finds the four true regressors, and 64 network models find the true three-connection graph. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-487](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-487.md)); worth reading as the source of Bayesian model reduction: if a set of models differ from a full model only in their priors, the evidence of each is the full model's evidence times the posterior expectation of the prior ratio (Eq. 3), so one inversion scores them all. Under Gaussian (Laplace) posteriors the reduced free energy is closed-form (Eq. 9). The Savage–Dickey ratio is the point-mass special case (Eq. 6), and ARD and model selection are the same evidence maximisation over prior hyperparameters. The demonstrations are simulations, and whether the reduced free energy of a nonlinear model is a good proxy for the free energy of the reduced model is left open by the authors. |
| [LIT-626](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-626.md) | Three types of phenomenal consciousness and their functional roles: unfolding the ALARM theory of consciousness | Newen & Montemayor (2025), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 380:20240314. The ALARM theory: phenomenal consciousness has two levels of experience and three functions. Basic arousal, realisable without cortex, alarms the body when a homeostatic variable leaves its tolerance range, overriding slow regulation with no choice involved; it adds lasting care for the injury and one-shot, generalised avoidance learning. General alertness, cortical and attention-guided, enables flexible learning and decision-making. Reflexive self-consciousness is general alertness with metacognitive self-relational content, not a third kind of experience, and enables long-term planning that accounts for one's own and others' mindsets. IIT, higher-order theories and GNWT are faulted for tying consciousness to neocortex and leaving basic arousal out. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-489](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-489.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the ALARM theory: phenomenal consciousness has two levels of experience, basic arousal (subcortical, an alarm that overrides slow homeostatic regulation) and general alertness (cortical, attention-guided, for flexible learning and choice), plus reflexive self-consciousness, which is general alertness with metacognitive self-relational content and its own function, long-term planning. Its evidence is a short list of cited findings (hydranencephaly, decorticate cats, central lateral thalamus stimulation in macaques), and the functional claims are argued, not tested. |
| [LIT-628](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-628.md) | Homeostatic feelings and the biology of consciousness | Damasio & Damasio (2022), Brain 145(7):2231–2235, an Essay. Consciousness occurs when mind contents are spontaneously identified as belonging to their organism, and a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings (hunger, pain, well-being, plain feelings of existence) supplies that identification and "lends" consciousness to exteroceptive images. Feelings are hybrid: interoceptive pathways are unmyelinated, partly non-synaptic and unprotected by a blood–brain barrier, so the body and its neural map interact directly. Posterior brainstem lesions abolish consciousness where large cortical ones may not; consciousness needs "a partnership of nervous systems with the bodies they serve". | Active — skimmed 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-507](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-507.md)): every section was covered, but through a fetch tool that returned section-by-section accounts with short quotes, not a verbatim copy, so the quotes are unchecked; worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the Damasios' claim that consciousness is the spontaneous identification of mind contents as one's own, supplied by a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings, which are hybrid: in interoception the map and the body it maps interact and "commingle". It is a five-page Essay with no data. Its evidence is clinical and cited (brainstem coma versus cortical lesions, general anaesthesia), and its mechanism is the cellular contrast in Table 1: unmyelinated, non-synaptic, barrier-free interoceptive pathways. |
| [LIT-629](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-629.md) | Two neural correlates of consciousness | Block (2005), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 9(2):46–52. There are at least two neural correlates of consciousness: a phenomenal NCC, the minimal basis of an experience's content (recurrent activation of MT/V5 with V1 for seen motion), and an access NCC, frontoparietal activation that broadcasts the content in a global workspace. Because access is a winner-take-all competition, a recurrent sensory representation can lose and stay unaccessed. Signal-detection analyses of exclusion tasks and of V1 figure–ground modulation in monkeys suggest experience without access. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-496](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-496.md)); worth reading as the short empirical turn of Block's distinction: a phenomenal NCC (recurrent activity in sensory areas, such as MT/V5 with V1 for seen motion) and an access NCC (frontoparietal broadcasting), with a winner-take-all contest for access as the reason the first can occur without the second. Its evidence is signal-detection reasoning: Supèr et al.'s V1 figure–ground modulation persists when low salience or many catch trials uncouple it from the monkey's saccade. The case is suggestive, "a glimmer", and the later papers make it at length. |
| [LIT-631](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-631.md) | Conscious Processing and the Global Neuronal Workspace Hypothesis | Mashour, Roelfsema, Changeux & Dehaene (2020), Neuron 105(5):776–798. A review of the global neuronal workspace hypothesis by its proponents. Conscious access is a sudden, non-linear ignition of a distributed network of long-range pyramidal neurons, with prefrontal cortex a key hub, that amplifies, sustains and broadcasts one representation; unseen stimuli produce only a decaying wave. Evidence: a late (>200–300 ms) divergence between seen and unseen trials across modalities, prefrontal ignition in monkeys tied to the signal-detection threshold, and the disconnection of frontal-parietal networks by every major class of anaesthetic. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-510](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-510.md)); worth reading as the record's first source statement of the global neuronal workspace (GNW): conscious access is a non-linear "ignition" in which recurrent loops among long-range prefrontal, parietal and other hub neurons amplify, sustain and broadcast one representation to the brain's specialised processors. Its strongest evidence is van Vugt et al.'s (2018) monkey recordings, where seen and unseen stimuli both drive V1 and V4 but only seen ones (and false alarms) ignite sustained prefrontal firing, and the signal-detection threshold maps onto the ignition threshold. It is a review by the theory's proponents, explicitly a theory of access, and it concedes that the four leading theories cannot yet be told apart experimentally. |
| [LIT-632](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-632.md) | Comparing the Major Theories of Consciousness | Block (2009), in Gazzaniga (ed.), The Cognitive Neurosciences, 4th ed., MIT Press, ch. 77, pp. 1111–1122. Compares the three theories neuroscientists take most seriously: higher-order thought, the global workspace and the biological theory. Only the biological theory fully acknowledges the explanatory gap; the others replace it with a puzzle their own theory creates. Concept dualism stops the gap becoming dualism. The ambitious higher-order theory also fails on stipulation, mismatch and infants. Integrated information is criticised as a theory of intelligence. The biological theory is the least friendly to machine consciousness. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-505](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-505.md)); worth reading as Block's comparison of the higher-order thought, global workspace and biological theories by one test: does the theory recognise the explanatory gap? The ambitious higher-order theory and the workspace theory turn the gap into a puzzle of their own making, so only the biological theory "fully acknowledges" it; concept dualism keeps that from becoming dualism. Also the source of the "biological theory" that Chalmers's meta-problem paper cites as "Block 2009", and a short argument that the biological theory is less friendly to machine consciousness than its rivals. |
| [LIT-633](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-633.md) | Cross-region neuron co-firing mediated by ripple oscillations supports distributed working memory representations | Verzhbinsky, Daume, Cheng, Rutishauser & Halgren (2026), Nature Neuroscience 29:2566–2577. In 1,373 single units from hippocampus, amygdala, vmPFC, ACC and preSMA of 35 epilepsy patients doing a Sternberg task, ripples (70–100 Hz) co-occur between bundles up to about 220 mm apart with no decline beyond the local bundle, and cross-region unit co-firing rises about 30% during co-ripples. That rise exceeds a rate-only null (STTC 117% higher), grows with memory load, and co-ripples hold more repetitions of a stimulus's encoding co-firing at retrieval, more on fast trials. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-494](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-494.md)); worth reading as single-unit evidence that brief co-occurring ~90 Hz ripples in distant human forebrain sites (up to about 220 mm, across hemispheres) mark windows of raised cross-region co-firing, about 30% above no-ripple periods and beyond what firing rates alone predict, that this scales with working-memory load, and that stimulus-specific co-firing from encoding recurs more often inside co-ripples at retrieval, most of all on fast trials. One reanalysed open dataset (35 patients, one Sternberg task, load 1 versus 3), clinically placed electrodes, and correlational throughout: nothing perturbs the ripples. |
| [LIT-636](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-636.md) | The Border Between Seeing and Thinking | Block (2023), Oxford University Press, open access. Argues, by Block's own précis ([LIT-649](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-649.md)), that perception is constitutively iconic, nonconceptual and nonpropositional while cognition is paradigmatically discursive, conceptual and propositional, using scientific marks of perception such as adaptation; that core cognition splits between the two; and, in a chapter on consciousness, against cognitive theories of consciousness. Unread: seeded from the chapter list and the précis. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-03 from Crossref's book and chapter records and from Block's own précis ([LIT-649](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-649.md)), not read. The book is open access at Oxford University Press under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Unpaywall lists the OUP book PDF), so a lawful full text exists, but academic.oup.com answered every request with a Cloudflare "Just a moment..." challenge, and OAPEN and DOAB, which normally mirror such books, refused this session's requests; I did not try to get past either. The précis was read in its place. Filed because the record cites the book twice ([NOTE-104](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-104.md) for pp. 454–458 on the neural replacement argument, [NOTE-150](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-150.md) for the perception–cognition border), and those citations need a code. A human reader can open the OUP copy, and a reading would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-637](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-637.md) | What Is Wrong with the No-Report Paradigm and How to Fix It | Block (2019), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 23(12):1003–1013. Whether perceptual consciousness needs prefrontal circuits cannot be settled by no-report paradigms, because subjects not asked to report may still think about what they see, and that thought tracks the percept. A no-post-perceptual-cognition paradigm is needed. Brascamp et al.'s rivalry with inconspicuous switches is one, and it found no detectable prefrontal difference. Box 2 argues that binocular rivalry is driven by local features, against the predictive-processing account. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-495](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-495.md)); worth reading as the argument that removing report does not isolate the neural basis of conscious perception, because subjects, monkeys included, can still think about what they see ("the bored monkey problem"). What is needed is a paradigm with no post-perceptual cognition that differs between percepts. Brascamp et al.'s inconspicuous binocular rivalry, whose switches subjects could not tell from constant random changes, is offered as one, and found no prefrontal difference by fMRI. Block flags that fMRI may be too coarse, and that ECoG could still favour prefrontalism. |
| [LIT-638](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-638.md) | Interacting spiral wave patterns underlie complex brain dynamics and are related to cognitive processing | Xu, Long, Feng & Gong (2023), Nature Human Behaviour 7:1196–1215. In Human Connectome Project fMRI (100 subjects per cohort), the phase field of slow cortical fluctuations holds about 16–19 rotating spirals at a time, centred on phase singularities that drift superdiffusively and sit on boundaries between functional regions. Opposite spirals annihilate, like ones repel. Spiral locations and rotation directions decode four language-task conditions at about 48% (chance 25%, matched raw-signal decoder 30%), and spiral arrays route task activity flow bottom-up while listening and top-down while answering. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-502](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-502.md)); worth reading as the claim that slow (0.01–0.1 Hz) human cortical fMRI fluctuations self-organise into many mobile, interacting spiral waves around phase singularities, as in excitable media and turbulence, and that their locations and rotation directions are task-specific and steer large-scale activity flow. The detection is careful about filtering artefacts (phase-randomised null, filtered–unfiltered similarity); the functional claims are correlational, the spatial scale was chosen to maximise task decoding, and the "gate" and "wall" rules are read off streamlines and a phase-oscillator lattice, not tested by perturbation. |
| [LIT-640](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-640.md) | Perceptual consciousness overflows cognitive access | Block (2011), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 15(12):567–575. A defence of the overflow argument: perceptual consciousness has a higher capacity than cognitive access. Critics who call it an illusion must posit detailed unconscious iconic memory and conscious generic or fragmentary representations, for which there is no independent evidence. Fragile visual short-term memory, a cortical store of about 5–7 of 8 items over 1–4 s that attention and dlPFC TMS spare while they impair working memory, supports rich perception. Overflow means most items are not accessed, not that any is inaccessible. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-500](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-500.md)); worth reading as Block's reply to the anti-overflow critics of 2009–2011. Sparse views must posit an unconscious iconic memory detailed enough to do the Sperling and Amsterdam tasks plus conscious "generic" letters or rectangles, and Block argues there is no independent evidence for either. It adds fragile visual short-term memory (about 6–7 of 8 items at 1–2.5 s, cortical, in V4, spared by right dlPFC TMS that impairs working memory) and an imagery task as support. Read from the in-press version. |
| [LIT-644](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-644.md) | Distinct ventral stream and prefrontal cortex representational dynamics during sustained conscious visual perception | Vishne, Gerber, Knight & Deouell (2023), Cell Reports 42:112752. Ten patients with subdural electrodes watched images for 300–1,500 ms with no report on analysed trials. High-frequency activity dropped about 80% after onset in every region, but category and exemplar information in ventral temporal cortex stayed decodable and time-invariant for as long as the image stayed on. Prefrontal and parietal information was a transient burst at about 150–600 ms that did not track duration. Both IIT's and the global workspace's predictions for this paradigm held. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-499](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-499.md)); worth reading as the cleanest test in the record of what neural activity does while a seen image simply stays on. In 10 epilepsy patients with subdural electrodes, high-frequency activity falls about 80% after onset everywhere, yet category and exemplar information in ventral temporal (and less robustly occipital) cortex stays decodable, time-invariant and as long as the image, while prefrontal and parietal information is a transient burst at onset that ignores duration, with no report required. It confirms the multi-duration predictions both IIT and the global neuronal workspace made for this paradigm. Sparse frontal coverage and above-threshold stimuli only. |
| [LIT-646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-646.md) | Consciousness, accessibility, and the mesh between psychology and neuroscience | Block (2007), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 30(5–6):481–499, with open peer commentary. To find the neural basis of experience we must decide whether it includes the machinery of cognitive access, and reports seem unable to decide that. Inference to the best explanation can. Sperling, Landman et al. and Sligte et al. show phenomenology overflowing a working memory of about four items. If the workspace is not part of the basis of phenomenology, strong losing coalitions in sensory cortex realise that overflow; the mesh between psychology and neuroscience favours that assumption. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-497](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-497.md)); worth reading as the overflow argument and the paper that framed the methodological problem the no-report paradigm was built to solve. Phenomenology overflows cognitive access: in Sperling, Landman et al. and Sligte et al. subjects see 8–32 items and can access about 4. If the neural basis of phenomenology excludes the frontal workspace, strong but losing recurrent coalitions in the back of the head explain that overflow, and a better mesh between psychology and neuroscience is reason to accept the assumption. The target article was read; the 32 commentaries and the response were not. |
| [LIT-647](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-647.md) | Neural traveling waves in cortex: Network mechanisms and potential roles in neural computation | Muller, Busch, Davis & Reynolds (2026), Neuron 114:3156–3174. A review of neural traveling waves within single cortical areas, chiefly visual cortex: how circuits generate them, and how, by embedding sensory history in the evolving activity across a sensory map, they may implement spatiotemporal computations such as predicting upcoming input. It ends with a framework for generative processing by waves over sensory maps. Unread: registered from the abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the PubMed abstract, keywords and the Crossref record, not read. No lawful full text could be found: the article is not open access at Cell Press (Crossref gives the accepted manuscript an Elsevier open-access licence only from 2 September 2027), it is not in PubMed Central, Europe PMC lists no preprint, arXiv has none under Muller with this title, Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no repository copy, and Semantic Scholar marks it closed. The cell.com page returned a bot challenge, which was not pursued. A human reader with subscription access, or anyone after the accepted manuscript becomes open in September 2027, could read it and move this to Active. |
| [LIT-649](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-649.md) | Précis of The Border between Seeing and Thinking | Block (2024), Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 110(1):273–283, the précis for a symposium on his 2023 book. The book's main claim is that perception is constitutively iconic, nonconceptual and nonpropositional, while cognition is paradigmatically discursive, conceptual and propositional and can use perceptual material inside a "cognitive envelope". The global neuronal workspace is reread as the mechanism of that envelope, the conceptualisation of percepts. Nine kinds of evidence show working-memory representations differ from perceptual ones and are task-dependent abstractions, which increases Block's doubt that "raw" percepts are used in cognition. Iconicity is defined by tracking and mirroring conditions after Shepard. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-498](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-498.md)); worth reading as Block's own short statement, stand-in for the book ([LIT-636](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-636.md)), of the thesis of The Border Between Seeing and Thinking: perception is constitutively iconic, nonconceptual and nonpropositional, cognition paradigmatically discursive, conceptual and propositional. Despite its title it is "an update", and most of it develops one idea, the "cognitive envelope": the global workspace is better read as a theory of how percepts are conceptualised than of consciousness, and recent working-memory evidence shows percepts are recoded, not held raw, when used in reasoning. It is too short to carry the book's arguments for the main thesis, which it states but does not argue. |
| [LIT-650](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-650.md) | Conscious birds | Maldarelli & Güntürkün (2025), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 380:20240308. A review arguing that birds show sensory awareness (bistable perception in pigeons; crow nidopallium caudolaterale neurons that follow the reported percept, not the stimulus) and graded self-awareness (magpie and house crow mark tests; pigeons and roosters that treat their mirror image as not-a-conspecific while failing the mark test). Checked against three theories, the avian brain meets the anatomical and physiological requirements of the global neuronal workspace (a hub-and-module connectome with NCL as hub) and of recurrent processing, while IIT's have not been tested (no PCI, no grid-like lattice found). The authors say the evidence does not yet allow a strong conclusion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-488](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-488.md)); worth reading as a short, current statement of the case for consciousness in birds and of what each of three theories (global neuronal workspace, recurrent processing, IIT) would need to find in an avian brain. Its strongest evidence is second-hand: crow nidopallium caudolaterale neurons that track the reported percept rather than the stimulus (Nieder et al. 2020). Its sharpest argument is that the bird's prefrontal analogue is nuclear, not laminar, so conscious report does not need cortical layering. The authors say the findings "do not allow for a strong conclusion". |
| [LIT-708](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-708.md) | Rarely categorical, highly separable representations along the cortical hierarchy | Posani, Wang, Muscinelli, Paninski & Fusi (2026), Nature. In the IBL Brainwide Map (about 14,000 cortical units, 43 regions, mice doing one biased-block visual decision task), neurons' selectivity to eight task variables beats a covariance-matched Gaussian null for clustering only in VISp, AUDp and SSp-ul (4,617 selective neurons; regions with ≥ 50). Pooled modules and the whole cortex do cluster, with clusters tracking anatomy. Once conditions an area cannot tell apart are merged (5 to 16 of 16 remain), ≥ 95% of random balanced dichotomies are linearly decodable above a shuffle null in 15 of 16 analysed regions; GU is 0.82. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-549](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-549.md)); the record's first brain-wide test of whether neurons within a cortical area come in discrete functional types or form a continuum of mixed selectivity. In mouse cortex during one overtrained decision task, a covariance-matched Gaussian null is beaten within single areas only in a few primary sensory ones, while the task conditions each area tells apart are linearly separable in nearly every balanced split. Neuron types appear when areas are pooled, and track anatomy. Second reading under [ADR-013](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-013.md); the anthology holds it as [ANTH-LIT-696](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/blob/main/record/literature.d/LIT-696.md), read for concept geometry in ML. |
| [LIT-832](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-832.md) | Explaining the Brain: Mechanisms and the Mosaic Unity of Neuroscience | Craver (2007), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199299317.001.0001. Good explanations in neuroscience describe mechanisms; a component is constitutively relevant to a mechanism's behaviour when it is a part of the mechanism and the two are mutually manipulable, which is distinct from causal relevance between events; neuroscience is unified as a mosaic of constraints across levels, not by reduction. Unread: registered from metadata and reviews. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-07 from Crossref's records (monograph and chapter list) and published reviews, not read: the book is paywalled at Oxford Academic. Filed because the owner's essay "The Organization of Will" cites it for mechanistic explanation and for the difference between constitutive and causal relevance. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-872](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-872.md) | Hyperbolic geometry of the olfactory space | Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018), Science Advances 4(8):eaaq1458. In four natural odour sources the rank order of correlations between compound concentrations has the clique-topology signature of points near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball and not of a uniform Euclidean cube, and human perceptual descriptions of 127 odorants have that of a full 3D hyperbolic ball. Pleasantness, boiling point and acidity read out as linear axes of the fitted fruit-odour space. The hierarchy that motivates the hyperbolic model is argued from biochemistry, not recovered from the data. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-672](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-672.md)); worth reading as the first application of clique topology to stimulus statistics rather than neural data, and as the Sharpee lab's first claim of a hyperbolic geometry in biology. For four natural odour sources (strawberry, tomato, blueberry, mouse urine; 45–78 compounds over 50–101 samples), the rank order of absolute concentration correlations gives Betti curves that match points sampled near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball (R_max = 7, R_min = 0.9 R_max, the same for all four) and reject uniform Euclidean cubes of any dimension tried. Human descriptor profiles for 127 odorants (Dravnieks) match a full 3D hyperbolic ball and no Euclidean cube. Linear axes for pleasantness, boiling point and acidity are found in the fitted fruit-odour space. The tree that motivates the hyperbolic model is argued, not recovered: compounds do not cluster by chemical class, and the only null geometry is a uniform Euclidean cube. |
| [LIT-875](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-875.md) | An argument for hyperbolic geometry in neural circuits | Sharpee (2019 online), Curr. Opin. Neurobiol. 58:101–104. A four-page review arguing that neural and other biological circuits should have hyperbolic geometry, because hyperbolic space approximates trees, hyperbolic networks are navigable, and Zipf's law, read as states growing exponentially with log-improbability and taken as the mark of maximally informative, latent-driven systems, shares that exponential growth. Its evidence is the olfactory embedding of Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018) and earlier perception work; the Zipf-to-hyperbolic link is an analogy, not a derivation. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-670](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-670.md)); worth reading as the short programmatic statement, by the lab behind the olfactory and hippocampal hyperbolic findings, of why hyperbolic geometry should be expected in neural circuits, and as a map of the literatures it joins: hyperbolic random graphs and greedy routing, Zipf's law and statistical criticality, and maximally informative representations. Its own argument is a chain of analogies, not a derivation. Zipf's law is rewritten as a count of states growing exponentially with energy (−log probability), and exponential growth of states is a hallmark of trees and of hyperbolic space, so the two are said to be connected; but exponential growth of states holds for any system with extensive entropy, and what singles out Zipf (unit slope) plays no part in the step to geometry. A rigidity argument for three dimensions cites Mostow's theorem, which concerns finite-volume hyperbolic manifolds of every dimension ≥ 3 and says nothing about point clouds. The one piece of data, a 3D Poincaré-ball embedding of fruit odorants with a pleasantness gradient, is reproduced from Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018). |
| [LIT-876](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-876.md) | Hippocampal spatial representations exhibit a hyperbolic geometry that expands with experience | Zhang, Rich, Lee & Sharpee (2022 online, Nat. Neurosci. 26, 2023). The pairwise correlations of rat dorsal CA1 place cells have the topological signature of points sampled uniformly from a three-dimensional hyperbolic ball, not of a low-dimensional Euclidean cube, and the ball's radius grows with the logarithm of exploration time. Place-field sizes are near exponential, and in a Poisson model exponential sizes carry more positional Fisher information than uniform or log-normal ones, with an optimal radius that matches the measured one for the number of CA1 neurons. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-668](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-668.md)); worth reading as, on its own account, the first evidence that neural responses, not stimuli, carry a hyperbolic geometry. Pairwise spike-train correlations of a few dozen active dorsal CA1 cells per session (34 to 56 in the sessions shown), in rats on a novel 48-m track, a 2.5-m track and a 1.8-m box, give Betti curves (clique topology, invariant to any monotone transform of the correlations) that match points sampled uniformly from a 3D hyperbolic ball and fail to match uniform samples from Euclidean cubes of low dimension or shuffled spikes. The fitted radius (10.5–15.5 in units of inverse curvature) grows with the logarithm of exploration time, on scales from seconds to days, as the maximal information acquirable does. Place-field sizes are close to exponential, as the model requires, and in simulation exponentially distributed field sizes give more Fisher information than uniform or log-normal ones, with an optimal radius growing as log N that extrapolates to the radius measured. The "hierarchy" is one of nested place-field sizes; no tree is recovered from the data, and the only null geometry tested is Euclidean with uniform sampling. |
